items.text: Angellica Bell, 50, has learned some surprising new skills in midlife – and the brain-health benefits are huge
items.article: Trying new things in midlife could protect you from Alzheimer's as well as being fun - and it's TV presenter Angellica Bell's approach to getting older When was the last time you challenged yourself to try something new? Finding the time between work and life to pick up a new language or learn to tap dance a la Catherine Zeta Jones may seem an impossible task. But stretching your brain to pick up new talents, doesn’t only make you sound more interesting down at the pub, it is officially good for your health. Not only can it raise your dopamine levels, give you a sense of purpose and help your mental health, scientists at Alzheimer's Research UK say keeping your brain sharp by trying new activities can potentially stave off the devastating disease. If anyone is up for trying something new in their 50s, it is Girlguiding ambassador and Celebrity Masterchef winner Angellica Bell. She overcame her habit of saying no to things as she moved into her Second Act and now there is nothing stopping her. “I do love taking on new challenges,” she tells Ateh Jewel on the Second Act podcast. “When I decided to try Celebrity MasterChef , that was a massive turning point for me. "It was great to win a trophy, but it was much bigger and deeper for me because that's the first thing I'd ever won.

A fiery five-hour council meeting took a personal turn when the Woollahra mayor revealed she looked up the value of a pro-housing advocate’s home during a debate over plans to add 9400 homes to Sydney’s eastern suburbs. There was only one item on the agenda at Woollahra Council’s extraordinary meeting on Wednesday night – to finalise how the council would respond to the most significant rezoning of the eastern suburbs in decades. Under state government plans unveiled last month , housing density would be concentrated around Woollahra and Edgecliff train stations, building towers up to 32 and 34 storeys. More than 10 pro-housing advocates spoke at the public forum and were met with staunch opposition and questioning from some of the 13 councillors who attended. The meeting featured numerous interjections and tetchy back-and-forth exchanges, and multiple points of order were called. At one point, Liberal mayor Sarah Dixson said she was “one word away” from calling an adjournment to turn the temperature down. About 40 minutes into the five-hour-long meeting, it was a personal question that almost tipped the temperature in the room to boiling point.

items.key: ai:how one man survived 438 days adrift at sea
items.text: How one man survived 438 days adrift at sea
items.article: After setting sail from Mexico, on what should have been a routine fishing trip, José Salvador Alvarenga drifted across the Pacific for 438 days. As José Salvador Alvarenga stepped gingerly from a patrol boat onto the dock in Majuro, the capital of the Marshall Islands, he looked nothing like the fisherman who had disappeared 14 months earlier . His hair hung in wild tangles, a thick beard obscured his face, and although he could stand, Salvador walked with the slow, cautious steps of someone much older than his 36 years. Fourteen months adrift in a tiny fishing boat had ravaged his body. He was weak, riddled with parasites, likely contracted from eating raw birds and drinking turtle blood, and his malnourished body had swollen with fluid retention. A nurse stayed close by Salvador, as he made his way onto dry land for the first time in 438 days. Behind him was Tom Armbruster, then the US Ambassador in the Marshall Islands, who was one of the first people to speak to him after his horrific ordeal. ‘He looked like somebody who had been out in the wild for quite a long time’, Tom, now an international consultant, tells Metro over Zoom from his home in Ithaca, New York State.

items.key: ai:i live in paris's most touristy quarter but escape to this medieval city
items.text: I live in Paris's most touristy quarter but escape to this medieval city
items.article: Located on the Seine, Rouen has its own Notre Dame and centuries of defining history, without the bustle and tourist traps of the capital Before I moved to Paris in September 2025, I had romantic notions about Montmartre’s winding cobbled streets, artists’ square and quaint cafés. I’d visited a few times and it seemed classically Parisian, with its own distinct village feel. Perfect, I thought, for a new start. I was moving from London, where I’d spent almost 10 years living in distinctly un-villagey areas – so Montmartre seemed the ideal spot to settle down. After almost a year in the area, however, I’m wise to the reality of living in one of the most touristy parts of Paris. The winding streets seem to be swallowed whole by tourists for much of the day – more than 10 million visitors schlep up the hill to see the Sacré-Cœur each year – and after dark, the low hum of cafés is replaced by the noise of all-night bars. The world feels like a difficult place at the moment, and it can feel very hard sometimes to find things to be thankful for; when we are overwhelmed, we have less capacity to notice and reflect on the good things. Yet, ironically, proactively cultivating gratitude is one of the things that can actually help us feel less stressed. Instead of seeing something as a problem, try to see the opportunities within it. Our brains are very receptive and what we read or write can alter our emotional system.

items.text: The Greater Manchester park that’s an ‘escape from the city’ ideal for an autumn walk
items.article: It feels a world away from the hustle and bustle of the city centre Over the coming weeks parks, gardens and outdoor spaces will turn into a sea of reds, oranges and golds as trees don their autumn foliage in preparation for winter. It’s a spectacle which occurs every year but never ceases to be impressive, particularly on bright October days and atmospheric misty mornings. Just like blossom in the spring, these displays can be fleeting so it’s a good idea to catch them while you can. Going for a walk in the autumn months can bring countless benefits too, particularly as the nights draw in. It can be tempting to stay inside and hunker down, but getting out into the fresh air can clear your mind and help set good habits as winter approaches. There are many places to experience beautiful autumn displays across Greater Manchester. Among them is Philips Park in east Manchester. Located in the valley of the River Medlock, this green space is just a stone’s throw away from the Etihad Stadium and Co-op Live, as well as the city’s newest developments, Medlock Square . Covering an area of 31 acres, Philips Park is actually one of Manchester’s oldest public parks, having opened in 1846. In fact it was among the world’s first municipal parks, and came about largely due to the work of MP Mark Philips, who lobbied for the creation of parks for the working people of the city. Energy will be the centrepiece of this Budget. The Iran conflict resulted in a significant rise in crude oil prices, putting a financial squeeze on households and motorists. Home heating oil cost about €900 for 1,000 litres last year but is now above €1,600. Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers said a lower rate of carbon tax on home heating oil is being considered, but warned the Government cannot entirely insulate consumers from rising global energy prices. items.text: Aerial house photos used to be in all rural homes, but my search for one was no easy task
items.article: In the days before Google Earth, it was fascinating to see a structure you knew so well from ground level from a brand-new, bird’s-eye view A friend recently became an official Irish citizen and, as I pride myself on being a considerate gift giver, I set about coming up with the perfect token to mark the occasion. This friend bought a home in the past few years and did a beautiful job on renovations, so I wanted to get something for the house. I weighed up several options, from homewares – maybe a Foxford throw or a piece of Brookwood pottery – to contemporary Irish art. Who wouldn’t want a Jen O’Dwyer original or a beautiful Domino Whisker piece? Then, on a visit to Kildare to my childhood home, it hit me as soon as I walked in the door. The one quintessential object my friend must have: a vintage aerial photograph of her house to hang in the hallway of said house. Perfect. The aerial house photograph is a rural staple, as common a sight as a copy of David Gray ’s White Ladder, an expired packet of iodine tablets, or A Woman’s Heart on cassette. The photographs were big business for decades in the last century, particularly in the 1980s and 90s, as enterprising photographers took pre-emptive shots from small aircraft and then hawked them door to door, no doubt bigging up the glamour associated with such a unique piece of art.
